newsitem.title: UK: UK output data confirm fragile recovery.
newsitem.headline: UK output data confirm fragile recovery.

text.p: A steady rise in UK manufacturing output in September confirmed Britain's recovery is spilling over into the industrial sector but it remains fragile and vulnerable to further rate hikes and a soaring pound.

"There are tentative signs of recovery in manufacturing, but the improvement is still fragile," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes. "A further rise in base rates, pushing the pound even higher, could threaten to derail the recovery."
Manufacturing output rose 0.3 percent in September giving a 0.2 percent year-on-year rise.
Output rose 0.7 percent in the third quarter, the first quarterly rise since Q3 last year, techncially lifting manufacturing out of its prolonged recession.
BZW economist David Hillier said the rise in output showed the recent pick-up in final sales was finally feeding through to increased production, rather than eating into stocks.
"We are through the adjustment process and from now on should see output rising fairly strongly, and that means better balanced growth for the economy," he said.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, agreed manufacturing output was likely to pick up in coming months.
"Business surveys suggest that order books and output expectations are picking up while the inventory burden is less severe than it was earlier this year," he said.
But economists agreed the manufacturing recovery was in no danger of sparking inflationary pressures. It could even be jeopardised if choked by a further near-term rise in rates.
"The trend in output is accelerating, but not at a fast enough pace to warrant any additional near-term rate hikes," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins.
"Indeed, some will still probably question the wisdom of last week's move."
Economists said Tuesday's data increased the likelihood that UK base rates would remain at 6.0 percent going into the general election, which must be held by May 22.
A rise in rates would launch a two-pronged attack on the fledgling recovery in manufacturing.
In addition to slowing demand and raising the cost of investment, it could push sterling even higher, threatening British manufacturing exports as they become more expensive.
Sterling has risen nine percent in the last three months. It has jumped over one percent since last Wednesday's surprise 25 basis point hike in interest rates.
The fastest growth in the manufacturing sector came from consumer durables which rose 1.3 percent quarter-on-quarter and 4.1 percent year-on-year.
"These account for just 5.0 percent of total production and a more broad-based revival will be needed to ensure industry enjoys a firm recovery in the coming months," said Loynes.

Economists pointed to the pick-up in consumer durables production as evidence that buoyant consumer spending, already seen in retail sales data, finally appeared to be filtering through to final output.
The Office for National Statistics said industrial output rose 0.5 percent in September, giving a 0.3 percent year-on-year rise, broadly in line with expectations.
